title: Writing away from the piano: Marion Evans, Strayhorn and Ellington
summary: Jones explains he writes away from the piano, learned that from Marion Evans and Billy Strayhorn, and compares Ellington's use of the piano.

story.theme_name: Writing and arranging: how musicians compose
story.community_name: Writing, arranging and composing: how the music gets made

blocks.x: You said something a few minutes ago about it being different when you weren't playing the material yourself, when you weren't at the piano.

Oh, yes. Well, I had to -- you know, the teachers that I studied with, it took me a long time to learn to write away from the piano. And it comes out much better, because your mind is much better than your hands.
It's a much wider scope, you know, and you just depend on your mind rather than your --
You don't write at the piano then.

Very seldom. In fact I was talking to Ellington about that once, and he still used the piano, not -- well, he kept it, you know, he kept it around his bed. To be sure that -- it's a thing to test what your mind is thinking about. You go back to it for a reference, to see if it sounds like you want it to sound.
Yeah. I'd see him jot down a few notes on a scrap of paper, but it would only go so far until he'd get to a piano to play those notes.
Yeah. Well, I had a good teacher, a fellow named Marion Evans, back east, and he was --

Yes. In New York. A brilliant arranger. In fact he's a brilliant man all around. And he taught me to get away from the piano, not to be insecure. And the other person who taught me that was Billy Strayhorn.
Because Strayhorn didn't use the piano that much.
I guess I was never around Billy when he was actually writing.
Yeah. I'd see him and Duke together, but -- working on things, but come to think of it, Duke would be at the piano and Billy would be across the room.
